title: Acoustic Design Criteria in Naturally Ventilated Residential Buildings: New Research Perspectives by Applying the Indoor Soundscape Approach
central_proposition: Applying an indoor soundscape approach can overcome the apparent conflict between natural ventilation needs and external noise intrusion in residential buildings, fostering wider adoption of natural ventilation as a passive design strategy that enhances user health and well-being.

concept_definitions.name: Soundscape
concept_definitions.definition: Integrates noise control engineering approaches with physical, social, and psychological approaches to reach a holistic characterization of the acoustic environment, its perceived dimensions, and its health outcomes, where sounds are differentiated based on people's perception, experience, and understanding of the acoustic environment, in context.

concept_definitions.name: Indoor Soundscape
concept_definitions.definition: Characterizes how people perceive, experience, and understand the indoor acoustic environment in the context of their working, living or leisure environments, with the building itself playing a fundamental role in defining the acoustic environment, people-related, and contextual factors.

concept_definitions.name: Alliesthesia
concept_definitions.definition: A 'changed sensation' where a given stimulus can arouse different sensations according to the stimulated person's internal state: pleasant when useful and unpleasant when useless or harmful.

concept_definitions.name: Adaptive Acoustic Comfort
concept_definitions.definition: A hypothetical model suggesting that a different noise sensitivity could be assumed under natural ventilation conditions, resulting in higher noise levels being tolerated due to lower expectations of low noise levels, appreciation of non-acoustic benefits, and different availability of control compared to mechanically ventilated buildings.

concept_definitions.name: Salutogenic Approach
concept_definitions.definition: A building design approach where the focus is more on 'peoples' resources and capacity to create health than the classic focus on risks, ill health, and disease.

argument_structure: The paper first reviews existing acoustic design criteria and façade noise control strategies for naturally ventilated residential buildings, identifying their limitations as a fragmented approach to Indoor Environmental Quality (IEQ) and a lack of perceptual perspective. It then introduces the indoor soundscape approach as a human-centered, contextual framework to address these limitations, proposing that it can reframe the conflict between ventilation and noise by valuing sounds perceptually. Finally, it suggests a research agenda to explore this new perspective.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: The core causal logic is that human perception of sound is not solely determined by decibel levels but is modulated by cognitive and behavioral factors (e.g., sense of control, connection to outside) and multisensory interactions (e.g., thermal comfort from airflow). By adopting an indoor soundscape approach, which underpins a perceptual perspective and contextualizes the experience, sounds can be valued as resources rather than just 'noise' to be minimized. This allows for 'positive acoustic alliesthesia' where sounds, even at higher levels, can be perceived as pleasant when associated with benefits like fresh air, thereby enabling wider adoption of natural ventilation for improved health and well-being.

findings.antecedent: Current acoustic design criteria (standards, guidelines, rating protocols) for residential buildings
findings.mechanism: These criteria primarily focus on minimizing indoor sound levels through noise reduction, typically without distinguishing for ventilation strategy, which creates an apparent conflict with the need for ventilation openings and thus impedes NV adoption.
findings.quote: Acoustic criteria have been based on indoor noise level reduction, typically without a distinction based on ventilation strategy.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Review of international standards and technical guidelines (Table 2) and building rating/certification systems (Table 3).

findings.antecedent: Fragmented approach towards Indoor Environmental Quality (IEQ) in acoustic design criteria
findings.mechanism: Acoustic criteria are set without considering how buildings are designed and operated to meet multiple, simultaneous needs (e.g., thermal, visual, air quality), making it difficult for NV buildings to meet strict noise limits compared to mechanically ventilated ones.
findings.quote: The fragmented approach towards IEQ has led standards, technical guidelines, and rating protocols to set acoustic design criteria that do not take into account how buildings are designed and operated to meet multiple needs that refer to areas of comfort other than acoustics (i.e., thermal, visual and indoor air quality).
findings.empirical_support_cited: Discussion of the AVO guide and Field's work [104,105] on the unfeasibility of NV under current acoustic criteria.

findings.antecedent: Lack of a perceptual perspective in acoustic design criteria (focus on decibel-based metrics)
findings.consequent: Comprehensive understanding of acoustic comfort in naturally ventilated buildings
findings.mechanism: Decibel-based metrics alone fail to capture the multiple cognitive and behavioral factors (e.g., connection to outside, sense of control) that influence perceived sound quality and comfort, thus neglecting potential 'adaptive acoustic comfort' opportunities.
findings.quote: The lack of a perceptual perspective has resulted in acoustic criteria that neglects the multiple cognitive and behavioral factors impinging on comfort in naturally ventilated residential buildings.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Analogy with adaptive thermal comfort models and criticisms of decibel-based metrics in literature [51].

findings.antecedent: Perceived control over one's environment (e.g., window operation) and connection with the outside (via ventilation openings)
findings.consequent: Adaptive acoustic comfort (higher noise tolerance, positive perception of acoustic environment)
findings.mechanism: These factors, analogous to those in adaptive thermal comfort, can modulate an individual's noise sensitivity and hedonic response, leading to a more positive perception of the acoustic environment even at higher sound levels, through 'positive acoustic alliesthesia'.
findings.quote: factors such as the connection with the outside and the sense of control over one's environment may induce 'adaptive acoustic comfort' opportunities that are worth investigating.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Analogy with adaptive thermal comfort, AVO guide's mention of non-acoustic benefits of open windows [79], and research on perceived control [121,122].

findings.antecedent: Application of the indoor soundscape approach (perceptual perspective, contextualization)
findings.consequent: Apparent conflict between natural ventilation needs and external noise intrusion
findings.mechanism: By shifting the focus from mere noise level reduction to understanding how people perceive and value sounds in context, the soundscape approach reframes the 'noise' as a potential 'resource' that can contribute to positive indoor environments, thereby resolving the perceived conflict and enabling NV.
findings.quote: the indoor soundscape approach provides a framework capable of overcoming the limits of the traditional noise control approach.
findings.empirical_support_cited: The overall conceptual argument of the paper, synthesizing previous critiques and proposing a new framework.

findings.antecedent: Natural ventilation (NV) under the indoor soundscape framework
findings.consequent: Function of NV solutions (beyond just air exchange)
findings.mechanism: This reframing allows NV devices to be valued and assessed not only for their ventilation performance and noise insulation, but also for their ability to transmit, block, or adjust outdoor sounds to provide connection with the outside, release wanted sounds, or mask unwanted ones, integrating with biophilic design principles.
findings.quote: Rethinking NV under the indoor soundscape framework means to value it as a strategy to transmit, block or adjust outdoor sounds to provide a connection with the outside, release wanted sounds, or mask unwanted ones, while enabling low-cost and low-energy cooling and ventilation.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Purely theoretical proposition, redefining the role of NV.

findings.consequent: Indoor soundscape approach (design for positive acoustic environments)
findings.mechanism: Both approaches share a common goal of shifting focus from minimizing risks and ill-health to fostering positive health outcomes and well-being by leveraging people's resources and capacities, making them conceptually aligned and mutually supportive.
findings.quote: This also aligns with a salutogenic approach to building design, where the focus is more on 'peoples' resources and capacity to create health than the classic focus on risks, ill health, and disease'.
findings.empirical_support_cited: References to Antonovsky [45] and Lindstroem & Eriksson [46] for the salutogenic concept.

findings.antecedent: Multiple simultaneous environmental factors (e.g., noise and heat)
findings.consequent: Human perception and performance (e.g., comfort, annoyance)
findings.mechanism: Environmental stimuli interact through addictive, synergistic, or antagonistic effects, influencing human perception and performance in complex ways that require a holistic, multisensory understanding beyond fragmented IEQ assessments.
findings.quote: Multisensory research addresses this issue by investigating interaction effects (i.e., addictive, synergistic, and antagonistic effects [106] or even synesthetic associations [107]), occurring between different environmental stimuli upon human perception and performance but this field of research is still not fully explored and, as such, not integrated into building design regulations and practice [106,108,109].
findings.empirical_support_cited: References to multisensory research [106,108,109] and the AVO guide's acknowledgment of the lack of evidence for combined noise and heat effects [81,110].

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: The effectiveness of NV devices in providing positive indoor soundscapes can be evaluated by assessing perceived control over the acoustic environment, provided contact with outside, and people's response to multiple environmental factors.

Indoor soundscape descriptors and indicators can be derived from laboratory or field studies taking into account the peculiarities of indoor soundscapes as compared with outdoor ones, such as: the presence of multiple outdoor-generated sounds combined with sounds generated indoor; the presence of a reverberant field; the specific task, depending on the building type or on the building area.

Research should investigate interaction effects and synesthetic associations on perception in the presence of multiple environmental factors, specifically in relation to overheating or breeze conditions, to understand comfort perception under different environmental conditions (e.g., change in thermal comfort perception under positive indoor soundscapes or change in acoustical comfort perception under increased air speed for cooling reasons in overheating conditions).
bridge_warrants: The paper draws an analogy between the established adaptive thermal comfort model and a proposed 'adaptive acoustic comfort' model, suggesting similar mechanisms of perception modulation based on context and control.
It proposes integrating soundscape methodologies into broader Indoor Environmental Quality (IEQ) research to achieve a more holistic understanding of human-environment interactions.
The indoor soundscape approach is presented as aligning with the salutogenic approach to building design, shifting focus from risk mitigation to health promotion.

The paper suggests connections between the soundscape approach and biophilic design strategies, particularly regarding the value of contact with the external environment and nature through ventilation.
methodological_critiques: Current acoustic criteria for naturally ventilated buildings are based on noise level reduction without distinction for ventilation strategy, creating an apparent conflict with ventilation needs.

The existing approach to acoustic comfort in NV buildings suffers from a fragmented view of IEQ, failing to consider multiple simultaneous environmental needs (thermal, visual, air quality) and their combined effects on occupants.

Acoustic criteria currently lack a perceptual perspective, relying on decibel-based metrics that do not fully characterize perceived sound quality and neglecting cognitive/behavioral factors like control and connection to the outside.
The mere use of different sound level limits is deemed insufficient to define criteria tailored to the complex user–building interaction under NV conditions.
Traditional annoyance models have primarily focused on disturbing source types, with little attention paid to 'wanted' sounds or sounds of preference.
model_structure: The paper proposes a conceptual framework (graphically represented in Figure 1) that positions the 'Indoor soundscape approach' as a means to 'Rethink NV' by addressing the 'Limits in current approach towards acoustic comfort in naturally ventilated buildings' (fragmented IEQ, lack of perceptual perspective). This rethinking then informs 'Suggestions for the Research Agenda' for 'Acoustic design criteria for naturally ventilated residential buildings' and 'Façade noise control strategies enabling NV'. The framework emphasizes the interplay between 'Building', 'Acoustic environment', 'Context', and 'People' as pillars of the indoor soundscape concept.
limitations: Research on indoor soundscape is still at an embryonic stage, and a fully functional indoor soundscape model ready for design application and standardization is not yet available.
The proposal for higher noise limits in overheating conditions (e.g., AVO guide) is not yet supported by scientific evidence on human response to combined heat and noise.
The concept of 'adaptive acoustic comfort' requires further investigation by the research community to define acoustic criteria that account for multiple cognitive and behavioral factors.

A main challenge is to provide comprehensive scientific evidence linking neural, physiological, psychological, and contextual factors with psychoacoustical indices to guide the design of positive indoor residential soundscapes.

paper_metadata.title: Acoustic Design Criteria in Naturally Ventilated Residential Buildings: New Research Perspectives by Applying the Indoor Soundscape Approach
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Acoustic Design Criteria in Naturally Ventilated Residential Buildings: New Research Perspectives by Applying the Indoor Soundscape Approach
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: The indoor-outdoor connection provided by ventilation openings has been so far a limiting factor in the use of natural ventilation (NV), due to the apparent conflict between ventilation needs and the intrusion of external noise. This limiting factor impedes naturally ventilated buildings meeting the acoustic criteria set by standards and rating protocols, which are reviewed in this paper for residential buildings. The criteria reflect a general effort to minimize noise annoyance by reducing indoor sound levels, typically without a distinction based on a ventilation strategy. Research has developed a number of solutions, discussed here, that try to guarantee ventilation without compromising façade noise insulation, but, currently, none have been adopted on a large scale. This concept paper highlights the main limits of the current approach. First, a fragmented view towards indoor environmental quality has not included consideration of the following acoustic criteria: (i) how buildings are designed and operated to meet multiple needs other than acoustical ones (e.g., ventilation, visual, and cooling needs) and (ii) how people respond to multiple simultaneous environmental factors. Secondly, the lack of a perceptual perspective has led acoustic criteria to neglect the multiple cognitive and behavioral factors impinging on comfort in naturally ventilated houses. Indeed, factors such as the connection with the outside and the sense of control over one’s environment may induce “adaptive acoustic comfort” opportunities that are worth investigating. The mere use of different sound level limits would not be enough to define criteria tailored to the complex user–building interaction that occurs under NV conditions. More holistic and human-centered approaches are required to guarantee not only neutrally but even positively perceived indoor acoustic environments. For this reason, this paper considers this apparent conflict from a soundscape viewpoint, in order to expose still unexplored lines of research. By underpinning a perceptual perspective and by contextualizing it, the indoor soundscape approach provides a framework capable of overcoming the limits of the traditional noise control approach. This could provide the opportunity to foster a wider adoption of NV as a passive design strategy that enhances user health and well-being, while enabling low-cost, and low-energy cooling and ventilation, thereby contributing to current climate change challenges.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: The paper proposes that by shifting from a purely noise-centric approach to a soundscape approach, which considers human perception, context, and meaning of sound, it is possible to develop more flexible and effective acoustic design criteria that facilitate the adoption of natural ventilation in residential buildings.

mechanism_chain.description: The paper argues that traditional acoustic design criteria, focused on objective noise limits, create a conflict with the implementation of natural ventilation, thereby hindering its adoption in residential buildings.

steps.from_construct: Traditional acoustic design criteria (e.g., strict noise limits)
steps.to_construct: Conflict with natural ventilation (e.g., opening windows for NV introduces external noise exceeding limits)

steps.from_construct: Conflict between criteria and natural ventilation
steps.to_construct: Designers and developers prioritize meeting acoustic criteria over implementing natural ventilation

steps.from_construct: Prioritization of acoustic criteria over natural ventilation
steps.to_construct: Reduced adoption of natural ventilation in residential buildings

stimulus_images.description: A diagram illustrating the proposed conceptual framework for integrating the indoor soundscape approach with acoustic design criteria for naturally ventilated residential buildings.
